en: The *Laghu-saṃvara-tantra* (*Herukābhidhāna*) Chapter 1: Verses 1–15 1.1 Homage to the Lord Heruka! I shall explain the *Saṃvara*, which is the supreme secret, the essence of all tantras, the great bliss, the ultimate reality, and the source of all success. 1.2 This is the king of tantras, the supreme among all; it is the secret of secrets, the most excellent of the excellent. It is the heart-essence of all Buddhas and the supreme means for attaining liberation. 1.3 It is the great secret, the supreme of secrets, the most profound of the profound. It is the sovereign of all mantras and the supreme of all vidyās. 1.4 It is the essence of all the Buddhas and the source of all the Tathāgatas. It is the supreme method for the accomplishment of the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*). 1.5 It is the supreme of all vehicles and the pinnacle of all paths. It is the ultimate goal of all yogins and the supreme state of the Vajra-holder. 1.6 It is the secret of the Buddhas, the secret of the Bodhisattvas, and the secret of the Vidyādharas. It is the secret of the world and the secret of the gods. 1.7 It is the secret of the nāgas, the secret of the yakṣas, and the secret of the rākṣasas. It is the secret of the piśācas and the secret of the pretas. 1.8 It is the secret of the asuras, the secret of the garuḍas, and the secret of the kinnaras. It is the secret of the mahoragas and the secret of all beings. 1.9 It is the secret of the three worlds and the secret of the ten directions. It is the secret of the past, the secret of the future, and the secret of the present. 1.10 It is the secret of the dharmadhātu and the secret of the *dharmakāya*. It is the secret of the *saṃbhogakāya* and the secret of the *nirmāṇakāya*. 1.11 It is the secret of the *svabhāvakāya* and the secret of the *jñānakāya*. It is the secret of the five families and the secret of the five wisdoms. 1.12 It is the secret of the six families and the secret of the six elements. It is the secret of the six sense bases and the secret of the six objects. 1.13 It is the secret of the six perfections and the secret of the six pāramitās. It is the secret of the six recollections and the secret of the six offerings. 1.14 It is the secret of the six mudrās and the secret of the six maṇḍalas. It is the secret of the six mantras and the secret of the six vidyās. 1.15 It is the secret of the six yogas and the secret of the six samayas. It is the secret of the six cakras and the secret of the six channels. It is the secret of the six drops and the secret of the six winds. It is the secret of the six syllables and the secret of the six letters. It is the secret of the six vowels and the secret of the six consonants. It is the secret of the six seasons and the secret of the six months. It is the secret of the six days and the secret of the six nights. It is the secret of the six times and the secret of the six moments. It is the secret of the six states and the secret of the six realms. It is the secret of the six destinies and the secret of the six births. It is the secret of the six sufferings and the secret of the six pleasures. It is the secret of the six attachments and the secret of the six aversions. It is the secret of the six delusions and the secret of the six ignorances. It is the secret of the six afflictions and the secret of the six obscurations. It is the secret of the six defilements and the secret of the six stains. It is the secret of the six impurities and the secret of the six impurities of birth. It is the secret of the six impurities of death and the secret of the six impurities of the intermediate state. It is the secret of the six impurities of the womb and the secret of the six impurities of the body. It is the secret of the six impurities of the senses and the secret of the six impurities of the mind. It is the secret of the six impurities of speech and the secret of the six impurities of action. It is the secret of the six impurities of the fruit and the secret of the six impurities of the cause. It is the secret of the six impurities of the effect and the secret of the six impurities of the condition. It is the secret of the six impurities of the result and the secret of the six impurities of the attainment. It is the secret of the six impurities of the path and the secret of the six impurities of the practice. It is the secret of the six impurities of the view and the secret of the six impurities of the meditation. It is the secret of the six impurities of the conduct and the secret of the six impurities of the fruit. It is the secret of the six impurities of the teacher and the secret of the six impurities of the disciple. It is the secret of the six impurities of the mantra and the secret of the six impurities of the mudrā. It is the secret of the six impurities of the maṇḍala and the secret of the six impurities of the initiation. It is the secret of the six impurities of the samaya and the secret of the six impurities of the vow. It is the secret of the six impurities of the deity and the secret of the six impurities of the self. It is the secret of the six impurities of the offering and the secret of the six impurities of the feast. It is the secret of the six impurities of the fire sacrifice and the secret of the six impurities of the torma. It is the secret of the six impurities of the recitation and the secret of the six impurities of the visualization. It is the secret of the six impurities of the yoga and the secret of the six impurities of the samādhi. It is the secret of the six impurities of the dhyāna and the secret of the six impurities of the samāpatti. It is the secret of the six impurities of the jñāna and the secret of the six impurities of the siddhi. It is the secret of the six impurities of the bhūmi and the secret of the six impurities of the pāramitā. It is the secret of the six impurities of the bodhicitta and the secret of the six impurities of the prajñā. It is the secret of the six impurities of the upāya and the secret of the six impurities of the karuṇā. It is the secret of the six impurities of the maitrī and the secret of the six impurities of the upekṣā. It is the secret of the six impurities of the śīla and the secret of the six impurities of the kṣānti. It is the secret of the six impurities of the vīrya and the secret of the six impurities of the dhyāna. It is the secret of the six impurities of the tathatā and the secret of the six impurities of the bhūtakoṭi. It is the secret of the six impurities of the abhāva and the secret of the six impurities of the nirvāṇa. It is the secret of the six impurities of the parinirvāṇa and the secret of the six impurities of the mahāparinirvāṇa. It is the secret of the six impurities of the dharmakāya and the secret of the six impurities of the rūpakāya. 1.1ab: Now, therefore, I shall explain the secret in brief, but not in detail.
1.1cd: The union with Śrī Heruka, which accomplishes all desires and aims;
1.2ab: The *Ḍākinījālasaṃvara*, which is even higher than the highest;
1.2cd: Abiding eternally within the secret, supreme, and delightful essence of all.
1.3ab: The being consisting of all ḍākinīs is Vajrasattva, the supreme bliss. 1.3cd:
For he is the self-arisen Blessed One, the Hero, the *Ḍākinījālasaṃvara*. 1.4ab: From the source, having emerged from the form of sound, they are the sphere of the conduct of the *samaya*.
1.4cd: It is difficult to find in the three worlds that which abides as the beginning, middle, and end.
1.5ab: Just like the union of the churning stick and the churning base, so too is it joined with mantra-recitation, meditation, and the like.
1.5cd: Listen to the yoga and the knowledge of the ritual procedures as they are proclaimed in the Tantra.
1.6ab: With the middle or superior breath, together with scented water, 1.6cd: one should always worship the Kulikā, and according to the specific time, the Dūtīs. 1.7ab:
The Dūtīs are innate (sahajā) and accomplished (siddhā), being inferior, superior, or middling.
1.7cd: With the mind focused within, one should meditate upon the accomplishment of desire.
1.8ab: One should worship the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas with the drops of one's own semen.
1.8cd: And by means of seeing and touching, as well as hearing and recollecting.
Cf. SaTaTaSa § 2651; GuSaTa 7.26 1.9ab:
"In this very way, one is liberated from all sins, there is no doubt;
1.9cd: the state of being a yogi is supremely meritorious, purifying, and the destroyer of sin."
1.10ab: One succeeds through the mantra of recitation, by means of recitation and meditation.
1.10cd: The practitioner, being well-composed, should constantly observe the rules of conduct (*samaya*).
1.11ab: However, if the rules of conduct are violated, success is not attained in the initiation mandala.
1.11cd: Honey mixed with blood and camphor, combined with red sandalwood;
1.12ab: Established in the midst of the Gaṇas, bearing the marks and signs of all the Vajras;
1.12cd: The knower of yoga should always lick [this] with the ring finger and the curved thumb.
1.13ab: Having tasted it like the drinking of soma, one attains eternal accomplishment (siddhi). 1.13cd: Herein, the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) become the instigator of all accomplishments.
1.14ab: Likewise, the fourfold worship consists of the heroes (vīra) and the yoginīs desired by the mind.
1.14cd: And the upholder of reality, having entered the non-dual union with the Hero; 1.15ab: Having condensed together that very bliss of divine and human states— 1.15cd:
even those do not equal a sixteenth part of that [bliss] by means of the diamond-essence.

1.15ab: In mountain caves and thickets, or upon the shores of the great ocean.
1.15cd: And in that primordial *śmaśāna*, one should draw the mandala;
thus ends the first chapter, on the entry into the mandala, in the *Herukābhidhāna*.

2.1ab: There, one should smear the ground of the mandala with the dregs of liquor and cow dung. 2.1cd: It should be joined with cremation-ground ashes and endowed with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta). (YoSa 9.4)
2.2ab: Having then smeared the ground, one should begin the mandala there.
2.2c: One should perform [the rites] in a cremation ground.
(YoSa 9.5ab)
2.3ab: With the charcoal powder of a city, combined with bricks from cremation grounds;
2.3cd: the preceptor, possessing excellent characteristics, should draw the divine mandala. (YoSa 9.5cd)
2.4ab: One who knows the system of right knowledge, [and knows the mantra of Śrī Heruka], 2.4cd:
free from anger, pure, skillful, a knower of yoga, and one who has reached the further shore of gnosis.
2.5ab: With hair made from skulls;
2.5cd: His limbs smeared with ashes, his body adorned with the various ornaments of Sambhu.
2.6ab: Standing upon a garland of bones, with his hair cut into a single lock; 2.6cd: Wearing a garland of bones as a pendant, holding a *khaṭvāṅga* staff in his hand;
2.7ab: Having made himself Śrī Heruka, he then attains the state of Śrī Heruka.
2.7cd: One should remember the wheel and place it in his heart; [one should place] *ab* [there].
2.8ab: Having thus armored oneself, one should assign the rampart and the directions.
2.8cd: Having thus armored himself, he should indeed place the weapon below.
2.9ab: He should place himself level with the wheel, but the mass of arrows above. 2.9cd: Having made for himself a cage that moves through the sky, he remains perfectly concentrated.
2.10ab: Having thus girded himself and donned his armor, he becomes impenetrable even by the gods. 2.10cd: Having thus well protected himself and adorned with mudrās and mantras, 2.11ab:
he should draw the formidable maṇḍala that bestows great siddhis.
2.11cd: Then, with a thread made from a corpse and dyed with great blood, 2.12ab:
one should delineate the formidable mandala, the supreme city of Heruka.
2.12cd: It should be one, four, or eight cubits in size, and perfectly square on all sides;
2.13ab: It should be provided with four doors and adorned with four archways.
2.13cd: The mantra-practitioner should wander and recite the *Ḍākinījālaśamvara* twice over.
Having established in its center [the mandala] which possesses petals and is radiant with a pericarp (*karṇikā*).
2.14cd: And with lotuses provided with filaments...
2.15ab: Upon the pericarp, one should place the Hero, terrifying with a great roar.
2.15cd: But [the form] consisting of fire has brilliantly radiant limbs and a great sound of boisterous, echoing laughter; 2.16ab:
adorned with a garland of skulls, divine, three-eyed, and four-faced.
2.16cd: And [he who is] covered by an elephant hide, with eyebrows split apart like a thunderbolt;
2.17ab: With a *khaṭvāṅga* staff in hand, adorned with half a garland of a hundred heads;
2.17cd: Standing before him is the goddess Vajravārāhī, most formidable.
Having visualized her facing Śrī Heruka as three-faced and of fierce form,
[one should visualize her] filled with the mantra of the skull-cup and dripping blood from her mouth.
Threatening all the directions, including the gods, asuras,
and humans, there are twenty-four ḍākinīs belonging to the Vārāhī family and the Saṃvara cycle.
2.20ab: One should worship within the center of the wheel, as well as in the cardinal and intermediate directions;
2.20cd: likewise, one should worship the heroes (vīra) stationed here upon the wheel.
2.21ab: If the practitioner desires non-dual success, he should worship the Hero.
2.21cd: Then one should fashion the water-pots (kalaśas), free from roots, black [substances], and the like;
2.22ab: Adorned with pearls, gold, gems, coral, silver, and copper;
2.22cd: And filled with all kinds of edible foods, they should be placed upon the skull.
2.23ab: One should wrap its neck with a thread and provide it with the tips of sprouts;
2.23cd: having placed eight [vases] at the doors, well-wrapped in pairs of cloths;
2.24ab: the ninth vase, wrapped in a pair of cloths, [should be placed] in the center.
2.24cd: Having fashioned silver or gold [images] adorned with jewels and pearls, 2.25ab: One should scatter all those beautiful objects made of gems and gold within the maṇḍala;
2.25cd: One should worship the delightful, supreme city; success will surely follow, there is no doubt.
2.26ab: Having sprinkled oneself with scented water from all sides, 2.26cd:
one should offer a hundred lamps to the east if one desires supreme accomplishment.
2.27ab: One should mentally place all the ḍākinīs in the sky above.

2.27cd: One should place all the *ḍākinīs* who are in the *bhūrloka* throughout the maṇḍala. 2.28ab: The knower [of reality] should place whichever *ḍākinīs* are in the *pātāla* within the *pātāla*. 2.28cd: One should assign all the Mothers (*mātaraḥ*) to the cardinal directions and the intermediate directions.
2.29ab: With flowers, perfumes, and likewise incenses, the practitioner who desires accomplishment should offer a hundred lamps.
2.29cd: He should worship the Vīras and Yoginīs situated within the maṇḍala of Śrī Heruka.
2.30ab: With banners that are red, yellow, white, black, and brownish-yellow.
2.30cd: With various garlands and wreaths, as well as with diverse kinds of garments; 2.31ab: And with canopies and beautiful bamboo-framed curtains;
2.31cd: One should provide foods to be eaten, chewed, licked, and drunk, remaining well-composed.
Thus ends the second chapter, the Chapter on the Ritual for the Worship of the Mandala, in the *Śrīherukābhidhāna*. 3.1ab:
Thereafter, the practitioner should first satisfy the master with his entire being.
3.1cd: One who desires accomplishment, being well-composed, should worship the Guru according to one's ability.
3.2ab: Taking up the sound of the bell, which is adorned with flowers and incense, 3.2cd:
the practitioner should ring the bell with a beautiful tone, or even a small drum, and let out the cry of "Hā hā!"
Having thus worshipped the mandala that fulfills all desires according to the prescribed rule,
and having covered the faces of those "spiritual sons" with a cloth, one should cause them to cast a handful full of flowers [into it].
Then, having performed a circumambulation, the practitioner, being well-composed,
should enter that beautiful, excellent city while taking refuge in Dakṣiṇāmūrti.
Then one should scatter a handful of flowers upon the maṇḍala.
Whichever [spot] that flower falls upon, one should designate that as the family (kula); one should show the sacred seats (pīṭha) of Śrī Heruka and the others.
Then, being well-composed, the preceptor should worship the mudrā;
on the second day, he should apply a sectarian mark (tilaka) to the disciples with blood over which the mantra has been recited three times.
3.7ab: Having uncovered the face, he should then show the mandala to the disciple. 3.7cd:
Whichever deity’s place it may be, he should point that out to him there.
3.8ab: Having then prostrated correctly, one should subsequently [enter] the city together with the preceptor; 3.8cd:
and having performed circumambulation again, one should proceed counter-clockwise (from the left) at the start of the return journey.
Having prostrated according to the ritual rules before the mandala and the guru,
one should then offer to the guru the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) as prescribed by the Tathāgata.
3.10ab: Having bestowed a hundred thousand pieces of gold and various kinds of jewels, 3.10cd:
as well as a hundred pairs of garments, elephants, horses, and even the kingdom;
3.11ab: and earrings, bracelets, armlets, and the most excellent finger-rings.

3.11cd: Having prostrated, he should offer his golden sacred thread, as well as his own wife or even his daughter; 3.12ab: Or a male slave, a female slave, or even a fire-altar (agni). 3.12cd: A wise man should offer himself to the guru with his whole being.
3.13ab: "From this day forward, I am your slave; I have surrendered myself to you. 3.13cd:
Having made such a firm resolve through these [words], the practitioner [proceeds].
3.14ab: Thereupon, the ḍākinīs and the mothers of yoga (yogamātṛ) become pleased with him.
3.14cd: The Ḍākinīs, Lāmās, Khaṇḍarohās, and Rūpiṇīs— 3.15ab:
With these Ḍākinīs, the practitioner should wander throughout the entire world. 3.15cd: All [beings] become his servants; of this there is no doubt.

3.16ab: For them, there shall be the accomplishment of yoga, through which the three worlds are unobstructed. 3.16cd: Invisibility, emerging from within a hole, the power of moving through the sky, foot-unguent, and then elixir— 3.17ab: these arise always and eternally at the will of the practitioner.
3.17cd: She assumes many forms and moves through space;
3.18ab: as a *ḍākinī* in particular, she subdues all living beings.
3.18cd: By practicing this yoga even once, the state of a yogin arises in an instant.
3.19ab: The yogi who, having not seen the maṇḍala, strives for the state of a yogi, 3.19cd: strikes at empty space with his fist and drinks a mirage.
3.20ab: This yoga is the best, the most excellent, and the supreme among all yogas.

3.20cd: Whoever shall desire [this], he, having overcome gods, asuras, and humans, will go [to the goal]. 3.21ab: He who is consecrated here in this mandala is a practitioner of all the tantras. 3.21cd: [The secrets are] the gopya, the īkṣaṇa, the pāṇi, the āliṅga, the dvandva, and so forth.
3.22ab: Therein, one shall be consecrated; this is the single supreme [tantra] among all tantras.
3.22cd: Whether in the *Tattvasaṃgraha*, the *Saṃvara*, the *Guhyasamāja*, or the *Vajrabhairava*, 3.23ab:
such a king of maṇḍalas has never existed before, nor will there ever be one again.
3.23cd: "Whatever has been stated and whatever has not been stated—all that resides within Śrī Heruka.
Thus ends the third chapter, the Chapter on the Ritual for the Right-hand Initiation, in the *Herukābhidhāna*.
Chapter 4 (based on the Sarnath edition)
4.1 Then the Ḍākinīs expand the worlds:
Mahāvīryā, Cakravartinī, Mahābalā, Suvīrā,
4.2 Cakravarmiṇī, Śauṇḍinī, Khaḍgarohā, and Cakravegā.
Khagānanā, Hayakarṇā, Subhadrā, and likewise Śyāmadevī;
Surābhakṣī, Vāyuvegā, and Mahābhairavā; Airāvatī, Drumacchāyā, Laṅkeśvarī, and Kharvarī.
4.4 Vīramatī, Mahānāsā, Prabhāvatī,
Caṇḍākṣī, and Pracaṇḍā— these are the accomplished ones (siddhās). The practitioner (sādhaka),
however, [should worship] first the twenty-four ḍākinīs beginning with Pracaṇḍā.
4.5–6. [Just as it is externally, so it is within oneself regarding body, speech, and mind:

The mantras consisting of the utterance of one's own name, joined with the syllables *hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ* at the end—having seen this supreme and most excellent yoga, one regards anything else as mere chaff.
The *Oṃkāradīpikā* bestows all accomplishments and fulfills all desires.
(4.7) Having seen the maṇḍala in the home, the perfected ones attained the state of heroes;
therefore, having understood this, one should constantly meditate upon it, for such is the word of the Tathāgata regarding accomplishment.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Non-duality of the Hero and the Yoginī," in the *Śrīherukābhidhāna*.
[Chapter 5 begins: Thereupon...
5.1 In the *Sarvadharmodaya*, the practitioner of mantra should, according to the rule, draw the universe upon the pericarp as the unstruck (*anāhata*) Śiva— the singular synthesis of all phenomena.
Herein are the words of the mantra:
5.2 Having brought together the *āli* and *kāli* and transformed them from their respective groups,
the best of sages should understand that which consists of four times four on the ritual diagram (*prastara*).
5.3 He should extract the Hero situated within the tantra, who accomplishes all desires and goals.
The fifth of the fourth, and also the fifth of the fifth;
the fourth of the fifth, and the third of the first;
likewise the twenty-ninth, and the first of the fourth.
5.5 Of the semi-vowels (*antaḥstha*), taking the fourth, then its second, as well as the thirtieth and likewise the twenty-sixth;
5.6 having extracted all this, and again the half of half of a hundred (fifty).
Then, taking the thirty-third [letter], the first of the first [group];
and the third of the semivowels (*antaḥstha*), and the third of the first [group]; and the thirty-second; and the fifth of the fourth [group]. 5.7
5.8 Of the fifth [vowel], that which belongs to the fourth; of the semivowel (*āntastha*), that which belongs to the first;

of the second [vowel], that which belongs to the third; and of the third [vowel], that which belongs to the first. 5.9 [The substitution is] the fifth of the fifth [vowel], but the first of the first [vowel].
Likewise, they know the eleventh and the sixteenth;
the first of the third [group], as well as the twenty-sixth,
the third of the fourth, and also the pair of sibilants (ūṣman).
5.11 The first of the first, likewise the twenty-seventh and the twenty-eighth; then the third of the first.
5.12 Also the fourth of the fifth—having taken these from the twenty-first.
Likewise the fifteenth and the twenty-fifth;
then the second of the first [group] and again the twenty-sixth;
the thirty-second syllable and indeed the very end of the sibilants (ūṣman).
Furthermore, the thirty-second, and again the fourth of the fifth [vowel],
the third of the second [vowel], and the fourth of the fifth [vowel];
and the third of the sibilants (*ūṣman*), and the thirty-seventh as the final one.
The first of the semivowels (*antaḥstha*) and likewise the twenty-first; the second of the semivowels and likewise the thirtieth;
the first of the fifth [class] and the first of the sibilants (*ūṣman*).
5.17 Likewise, [the first letter] of the fourth [varga] has the form of *dy*;
and that which is the first of the sibilants (*ūṣman*) is likewise the twenty-eighth.
5.18 But the second of the first [varga] is said to be the first of the third.

That which is the third of the first [group], the fourth of the fourth, the second of the semivowels (antaḥstha), and the fifth of the third; they call this the *vyākāra* "vīra. Likewise, that which is the fourth of the first and also the eighth.
The fifth of the fourth, the fifth of the fifth,
likewise the twenty-seventh of the fourth, and the fourth;
again the twenty-seventh, and likewise indeed the twenty-sixth.
Taking the twenty-fifth and the thirty-third,
as well as the fourth of the fourth and the fifth of the fifth; likewise, the fifth of the fourth and the first of the first, and also the twenty-seventh.

The fourth of the semivowels (*antaḥstha*), the twenty-first likewise, the second of the sibilants (*ūṣman*), and also the twenty-sixth; *Kara 2, kuru 2, bandha 2, trāsaya 2, kṣobhaya 2, hrauṃ 2, hraḥ 2, pheṃ 2, phaṭ 2, daha 2, paca 2, bhakṣa 2, O you who wear a garland of hanging entrails, blood, and fat! Seize 2 the serpent or snake dwelling in the seven netherworlds! Threaten 2! Draw forth 2! Hrīṃ 2, jṇoṃ 2, kṣmāṃ 2, hāṃ 2, hīṃ 2, hūṃ 2, kili 2, sili 2, hili 2, dhili 2, hūṃ 2.*
5.25 The mantra of the King of Vidyās is the most excellent of all means of accomplishment;
nothing superior to it exists within the three worlds.
5.26 Having known the mantra of Śrī Heruka, one should discard all other [mantras] like chaff, just as one discards woodworm-infested timber.
Thus is proclaimed the root mantra.
This concludes the fifth chapter, the procedure for extracting the syllables of the root mantra, in the *Śrīherukābhidhāna*.
[Chapter 6, based on the Sarnath edition]
6.1. Hereafter follows the twenty-two-syllable heart mantra and the seven-syllable subsidiary heart mantra;
likewise, the seed syllable is the eighth from the *ya*-group, accompanied by twelve measures (*mātrā*).
6.2. Having interspersed it with other syllables, the six-limbed Śrī Heruka is proclaimed.
Established in each individual syllable through the union with the six heroes—
Oṃ, Namaḥ, Svāhā, Vauṣaṭ, Hūṃ, and Phaṭ— the practitioner should know these as the heart-mantras. The first is indeed the heart, and the second is remembered as the head.
The third, however, should be given as the crest-lock (*śikhā*); the fourth shall be the armor (*kavaca*);

Thus ends the thirty-sixth chapter in the *Śrīherukābhidhāna*, the chapter on the ritual procedure for the attraction of reality-worship (*tattvapūjā*).
Now I shall explain another [practice], the sādhana for one overcome by a hostile deity:
the mantras and ḍākinīs, mutually entwined, are joined together in one place.
37.2 One should cause [the person] to vomit the food already eaten or that which was intended to be eaten by means of the mantra ending with the *udgītha*.
Then, after a full seven nights have passed, one should employ them in eating and other such activities.
37.3 By this means, they come under one's control for as long as they live; of this there is no doubt.
Having drunk the ghee of a tawny cow, one should induce vomiting at the conclusion of the recitation (japa).
Then, with that [ghee], one should anoint oneself and the face;
if [the person] is constantly angry, by showing [himself thus], one shall bring him under control.
37.5–6. Having prepared a *śaṅkulikā* (a type of cake) with unbroken sesame oil mixed with rice flour, the practitioner of mantra should employ it by means of consumption;
as long as one lives, [the person] will always be under control, provided they do not abandon the ritual.
Having eaten black sesame seeds mixed with *rājikā* and vomited them out, one should grind *kuṣṭha*, along with *apāmārga*, *karaja*, and *udarakiṭaka*,
with one's own blood and then saturate it with semen.
37.8 One should employ food, drink, collyrium, garments, and ointments for the purpose of subjugation; thus, there is no doubt that [the person] remains under one's control for as long as life lasts.
37.9 An oblation of cow-flesh is the fire-sacrifice (*homa*), and the deity should be smeared with its blood.
At that very moment, he comes under one's control; if he does not come, he dies.
Having visualized his flesh before oneself, the wise practitioner should perform the fire-oblation (homa).
At the conclusion of the oblation, having offered the sacrificial cake (bali), one may summon the three worlds in an instant.

Success shall be attained within seven nights. This characteristic of the conduct of the *samaya*, which is difficult to find in the three worlds, must always be guarded with effort by oneself through secret mantras.

37.12 "The one of little fortune does not obtain the hidden meaning, nor does he succeed with practitioners of meager merit; however, it is obtained by me when I am pleased. Thus ends the thirty-seventh chapter, the Procedure for the Internal Subjugation, in the *Śrīherukābhidhāna*.

38.1 Thereafter, [one should learn] the secret signs (*chommaka*) of the *ḍākinīs*, the characteristics of their bodies, and likewise the classification of the limbs of the heroes; that which is to be accomplished is indeed the attainment of success (*siddhi*).
38.2 Vīreśvara does not write it down, nor should he recite it before anyone;
it must be concealed in every way, well-guarded by those who follow the left-hand path (vāmācāra).
38.3 If the mantra-practitioner recites it through negligence, the ḍākinīs of secret characteristics will [punish him].

I do not see even a thousand *ḍākinīs* who could devour him in many ways; that evil-souled one is a breaker of the *samaya*, a man of wicked conduct, and a slayer of Brahmins— of this there is no doubt.
That evil-doer, deluded, deceived, and wicked-souled—
when he is being devoured by the yoginīs, I am not his protector;
in the midst of the guhyakas, that practitioner is nothing but a sacrificial animal.
38.6 He who betrays his guru and betrays the samaya is fallen from the world of the Buddhas;
but for him who protects the tantra of Śrī Heruka, whose appearance is formidable, 38.7 I, together with the ḍākinīs, shall bestow grace upon that fair-faced one.
The practitioners approve and conceal [the teachings];
he is always dear to the yoginīs, and for him there is no doubt regarding success.
The practitioner attains heroism and becomes the sovereign of the sky-goers in the three worlds.
38.9 The practitioner who desires the state of a hero becomes honored everywhere;
yoga proceeds for him, and he finds the oral tradition.
38.10 Upon seeing a heroic teacher who observes the vow of Śrī Heruka...

38.12 Having bowed with effort to that Great Hero who is constantly worshipped by all the Buddhas and others, he will undoubtedly be engaged in play. 38.13 Vārāhī resides in their hearts, established in the non-duality of the Heroine-Yoginī.
Because of the sight of that being of noble birth, by virtue of his merit,
[there appeared] on riverbanks, in the oceans, on mountains, and at crossroads—
[the section following "on mountains" has been reconstructed].

And in the Mahābhairava cremation ground and likewise in Pātāla, the Khecarī [is present];
together with those many terrifying and mighty Vetālas, the great hero sports as he pleases.
38.17 In hollows, caves, and secret places— hidden by human yoginīs—
she sports with the practitioner in those various locations and regions.
Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter, the procedure for the Secret Abode of Heroes and the Regions of the Yoginīs, in the *Śrīherukābhidhāna*.

39.1 Then the Mahāsiddhi-yogin, demonstrating the eightfold laughter-mantra (*hāsa-mantra*) to him, bestows it upon him; of this there is no doubt.
39.2 And by means of a terrible, loud sound, the *ḍākinīs* become fearsome.
Upon hearing that, they tremble and flee from that hero.
If the hero does not fear, even when together with the *ḍākinīs*,
he is then led by them to his own city, hidden in their left hands.
39.4 For one who desires the power of Śrī Heruka, Khecarī is led [to him]; delighting therein constantly, he shall go to Sukhāvatī.
39.5 Everywhere, the practitioner, whose body is mantra, is subject neither to old age nor death.
Thus ends the thirty-ninth chapter, the Chapter on the Ritual of the Terrifying Laughter of Vision, in the *Śrīherukābhidhāna*.

Next, I shall fully explain that by which one may bring a mortal under control; by means of this, a hero established in the ritual application of mantra attains success within a month.
40.2–3. Flesh combined with fish meat, even when consumed by one who is intoxicated,

grants the Lord of Heroes (*vīreśa*) to the practitioner great accomplishment (*mahāsiddhi*) within seven days, provided he is devoted to the fire-oblation (*homa*) at night, regardless of his current state.
If one performs the practice three times a day with exactly one hundred and eight [recitations], a king together with his army will be brought under control; with half that number, a heroic minister;
and with half of that again, a minister—one shall bring them under subjection within seven days.
40.5 One should offer oblations for the vassal kings thirty-two times according to the sequence of offerings;
for a Brāhmaṇa, one should offer twenty times over the course of seven days.
40.6 In this manner, one should offer seven times for a Kṣatriya and five times for a Vaiśya.

In the case of a Śūdra, however, there should be only three [offerings], but for one of the lowest caste (antyaja), he should offer only one. Having occupied a single seat, the heroic practitioner, by means of the power of the mantra, should thus attract all sentient beings according to the lineage of his family.

40.8 By acting in this way, a mortal hero who practices desire according to the prescribed rules and cultivates the yoga of the deities shall attain a fortunate aeon (bhadrakalpa). 40.9 The practitioner will become pleasing to the ḍākinīs; there is no doubt in this matter.

Thus ends the fortieth chapter in the *Śrīherukābhidhāna*, titled “The Procedure for Cultivating the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*) for Subjugation through the Five Colors. [This section is followed by 41.5cd in Professor Sanderson’s handout.]
Now, the supreme and most excellent rite, by which they understand subjugation,
summoning, inciting enmity, killing, expelling, and so forth.
41.2 Yawning, paralysis, delusion, and indeed pinning down; likewise, the seizing away of speech, as well as muteness, deafness, and blindness;
41.3 the causing of impotence, and also the transformation of one's appearance.
The practitioner should always accomplish these twelve great rites;
there is no doubt that success comes to the practitioner by mere recollection.
Among all the most excellent ones, the Ḍākinīs are omnipresent in the sacred seats (pīṭhas) and so forth.
41.5 Those who are born in various lands, endowed with knowledge within their own wombs,
are said to be the ḍākinīs; they are the mistresses of the vajra-maṇḍala.

45.1 Now follows the most excellent and supreme rite that accomplishes the siddhi of speech:
one hundred and eight red *karavīra* flowers.
Having collected [the substance], one should have it processed with cow's milk while reciting the mantra one hundred times.
One should strike the top of the *liṅga* with a flower over which the mantra has been recited once;
in this manner, one should perform the rite day after day for seven days, remaining well-composed.
Then, on the eleventh day, having gone to the great river, one should take flowers and cause each one to float away;
one should employ all of them in succession, reciting the mantra once for each.

Having taken a western flower from the river that has been carried upstream against the current, one should drink it mixed with water without touching it with the teeth; thus the practitioner becomes perfected through speech, as it has emerged from the Guhyatantra. 45.5–6.

45.6 Having bound the *yoginī-yogamudrā*, the mantra-practitioner, facing the person to be acted upon (*sādhya*), should recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times, [visualizing it] situated within the very belly of that person to be acted upon. 45.7 The wise practitioner, remaining focused on that [person's] mind, should move the little finger at the three junctions of the day.
Even a slayer of a Brahmin shall, within seven days, bring [the victim] under his control like Indra;
having fashioned an image of the person to be mastered from the powder of red sandalwood, one should smear its limbs with the three pungents (trikaṭuka) and beeswax.

45.9 Having pierced her at the secret place with a copper needle, the wise practitioner should heat her for seven days with smokeless charcoal of *khadira* wood. 45.10 By means of this [mantra] recited one hundred times, the king, together with his ministers and his domestic priest, [shall be subdued].
Then, one should quickly summon the inner apartments along with their retinue;
furthermore, one should write the name of the king together with his retinue upon birch bark,
interlacing it with the name [of the target], using the lac and yellow pigment of a *preta*.

Facing him, one should recite the mantra while heating [the object] with a fire of khadira wood in a cremation ground for the sake of accomplishment, until the beeswax melts. While it is being heated, it draws in even a king who is a universal monarch (cakravartin).
The practitioner, having combined the dust from the feet of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*), red sandalwood,
and ashes discarded in a cremation ground, [should perform the rite].

One should diligently heat it with smokeless charcoal of *khadira* wood; having rubbed that dust with both hands, one should offer it as an oblation until success is attained, for indeed, one takes up the very dust once the oblation has been performed.
Having restrained the breath, one should certainly bury there that [victim] who has been cast down;
she will surely become smokeless... [omitted in the manuscript, reconstructed from Tibetan].
Fainted, devoid of consciousness, afflicted, and utterly deluded.
45.17 It arrives with the speed of the wind and descends upon the practitioner;
he should employ either a *paśu* or a *dūtī*, and the wise one should distribute them.
45.18 Then indeed he should perform the rite, as well as the seizing of the *dūtī*.
Taking a fresh *karavīra* creeper the length of one’s arm,
the practitioner, having inscribed the mantra of whichever ritual he is performing upon it,
should then throw that creeper even into a blazing funeral pyre.
45.20 Then, having quickly seized her before she is consumed by fire,
one should whirl her around while recollecting Yama and reciting the mantra seven times.
45.21 At that very moment, she returns in her own form with the speed of the wind.
The practitioner, during the conjunction of the Puṣya asterism, should take a red karavīra flower over which the mantra has been recited one hundred times;
having smeared that flower with gorocana and placed it in water,
he descends into a great river and stands in water reaching up to his navel.

45.23 One should drink [the water] held within the hollow of the palms, over which the vidyā has been recited one thousand times, while both hands are filled with water. 45.24 Thereupon, success shall come to him; indeed, the practitioner attains mastery over speech.
One will certainly attract a king or a queen by means of the mind; one quickly brings gods, asuras, and humans under control,
and when enraged, can kill them with speech or even cause their eradication.
45.26 By means of speech, the practitioner effects restraint, thinking "it is thus indeed";
he may paralyze a river, a cart, or a machine by mere words, as well as the ocean. 45.27 Likewise, he may [paralyze] elephants, horses, clouds, a man, or even a bird.
With speech one performs all that is desired by the mind through the power of thought.
Now, for the practice of attraction which causes the infatuation of all women:
having gathered a red flower, one should take [a flower] of the *karavīra*.
45.29 One should place the flower, over which the vidyā has been recited seven times, into the middle of the womb; having enclosed it, one should apply that flower to the secret place.
45.30 The mantra-practitioner, possessing the yoga of non-dual knowledge, should recite the mantra one hundred and one times.
The practitioner should take one flower situated within the center of the *yoni*;
whoever he strikes with that flower shall instantly become submissive,
overwhelmed, deprived of consciousness, and subject to another's will in all the joints of his limbs.
45.32 And one quickly brings [the object] under control if the conviction returns;
this is the accomplishment of conviction, which unfailingly effects subjugation.
Thus ends the fiftieth chapter, titled "The Ritual for Attraction through the Accomplishment of Action and Speech of the Six Yoginīs," in the *Śrīherukābhidhāna*.

46.1 Now follows the [mantra] of the five *hakāra*s, which accomplishes all rites;
by the mere knowledge of which, accomplishment quickly proceeds.
46.2. Hā, hī, hai, hau, haḥ—these five *ha*-syllables, when placed in the hands, should be rubbed together;
even by the mouth of one who is thus impelled, blood flows forth at that very moment, and he shall kill the enemy.
46.3. One should rub dog’s blood contained in a skull-cup with the blood from one's own ring finger.
As long as the remainder persists, the one to be accomplished perishes.
(46.4) If, enraged and with bloodshot eyes, one recites the mantra with a blazing intensity,
one quickly kills a king along with his army, forces, and vehicles.
46.5 One should offer a bali-oblation of cats, mongooses, dogs, crows, cranes, jackals, and *ḍākinīs* into the fire;
for these bring swift accomplishment in this tantra, there is no doubt.
46.6 Having made a rope from the hair of rabbits and other such animals, one should empower it a thousand times with mantras.
Whomever one ties [this] around the neck becomes such [as described].
Having consecrated a hand a thousand times with mantras and joined it with *karavīra* flowers—one flower for each syllable—one should touch a pregnant woman.
The fetus is transferred; when released, there is liberation.
Whomever he threatens, he kills; furthermore, he causes them to be reborn.
Thus ends the forty-sixth chapter in the *Śrīherukābhidhāna*, the chapter on the ritual procedure for the five acts beginning with the syllable *ha*.
